title: No. 41 — General View of the Powers Conferred by The Constitution (Madison)
paragraphs: The Constitution the Convention proposed can be viewed in two general ways. The FIRST looks at the sum or quantity of power it gives the government, including the restraints it places on the States. The SECOND looks at the particular structure of the government and at how this power is divided among its separate branches.

Taking the FIRST view, two important questions arise. 1. Is any part of the powers handed over to the general government unnecessary or improper? 2. Taken all together, are they dangerous to the share of jurisdiction left to the individual States?
Is the aggregate power of the general government greater than ought to have been vested in it? This is the FIRST question.

Anyone who has listened fairly to the arguments against the government's extensive powers must have noticed that their authors have given very little thought to whether these powers are necessary means to a necessary end. They have preferred to dwell on the drawbacks that are bound to be mixed in with every political advantage, and on the possible abuses that go along with any power or trust that can be put to good use. This way of treating the subject cannot fool the good sense of the people of America. It may show off the writer's cleverness; it may open a boundless field for rhetoric and declamation; it may inflame the passions of the unthinking and confirm the prejudices of the misthinking. But cool and fair-minded people will see at once that even the purest human blessings contain some alloy; that we must always choose the GREATER good rather than the PERFECT good, if we cannot choose the lesser evil; and that in every political institution a power to advance the public happiness carries a discretion that may be misused and abused. They will therefore see that whenever power is to be conferred, the first question to settle is whether the power is necessary to the public good. If the answer is yes, the next question is how to guard as effectively as possible against turning the power to the public's harm.

To judge this subject correctly, we should review the several powers conferred on the government of the Union. To do so conveniently, we can sort them into classes by the objects they concern: 1. Security against foreign danger; 2. Regulation of the intercourse with foreign nations; 3. Maintenance of harmony and proper intercourse among the States; 4. Certain miscellaneous objects of general utility; 5. Restraint of the States from certain injurious acts; 6. Provisions for giving due effectiveness to all these powers.
The FIRST class contains the powers of declaring war and granting letters of marque; of providing armies and fleets; of regulating and calling forth the militia; and of levying and borrowing money.

Security against foreign danger is among the first purposes of civil society. It is an avowed and essential purpose of the American Union. The powers needed to achieve it must be entrusted, with real effect, to the federal councils.
Is the power to declare war necessary? No one will say it is not, so proving that it is would be superfluous. The existing Confederation gives this power in the fullest form.
Is the power to raise armies and equip fleets necessary? It follows from the power just discussed. It follows from the power of self-defense.
But was it necessary to give an INDEFINITE POWER of raising TROOPS as well as providing fleets, and of keeping up both in PEACE as well as in WAR?

The answer to these questions has already been anticipated elsewhere, too fully to allow a lengthy discussion of them here. The answer in fact seems so obvious and conclusive that it hardly justifies a lengthy discussion anywhere. How can anyone decently limit the force needed for defense, when he cannot limit the force of offense? If a federal Constitution could put chains on the ambition of all other nations, or set bounds to their exertions, then it might wisely chain its own government's discretion and set bounds to its exertions for its own safety.

How could readiness for war in time of peace be safely forbidden, unless we could forbid in the same way the preparations and establishments of every hostile nation? The means of security can be regulated only by the means of attack and the danger of it. In fact they will always be set by these standards and by no others. It is useless to put constitutional barriers in the way of the drive for self-preservation. It is worse than useless, because it plants in the Constitution itself necessary usurpations of power, and every precedent among them is a seed of unnecessary and repeated ones. When one nation constantly keeps a disciplined army ready to serve its ambition or revenge, it forces the most peaceable nations within reach of its schemes to take matching precautions. The fifteenth century was the unhappy period when military establishments in peacetime began. Charles VII of France introduced them. All Europe has followed his example or been forced to. If other nations had not followed it, all Europe would long ago have worn the chains of a universal monarch. If every nation except France were to disband its peacetime establishments now, the same thing might happen. The veteran legions of Rome could overpower the undisciplined courage of every other nation, and they made her mistress of the world.

It is just as true, though, that the liberties of Rome became in the end the victim of her military triumphs, and that the liberties of Europe, as far as they ever existed, have with few exceptions been the price paid for her military establishments. A standing force is therefore a dangerous provision, even if it is also a necessary one. On the smallest scale it has its drawbacks. On a large scale its consequences may be fatal. On any scale it is an object of laudable caution and precaution. A wise nation will weigh all these considerations. It will not rashly cut itself off from any resource that may prove essential to its safety, but it will bring all its prudence to bear on lessening both the need to resort to a resource that may be unfavorable to its liberties and the danger of doing so.

The proposed Constitution bears the clearest marks of this prudence. The Union itself, which it joins firmly together and secures, removes every pretext for a military establishment that could be dangerous. America united, with a handful of troops or not a single soldier, presents a more forbidding face to foreign ambition than America disunited with a hundred thousand veterans ready to fight. It was remarked on an earlier occasion that the absence of this pretext saved the liberties of one nation in Europe. Because her island position and her naval resources made her safe from the armies of her neighbors, the rulers of Great Britain have never been able, with real or invented dangers, to trick the public into a large peacetime establishment. The distance of the United States from the powerful nations of the world gives them the same happy security. A dangerous establishment can never be either necessary or plausible as long as they remain a united people. But they must never forget, even for a moment, that they owe this advantage to the Union alone. The day it dissolves will be the start of a new order of things. The fears of the weaker States, or the ambition of the stronger States or Confederacies, will set the same example in the New World that Charles VII set in the Old. The example will be followed here for the same reasons that made everyone imitate it there. Instead of drawing from our situation the precious advantage Great Britain draws from hers, America will look just like the continent of Europe. It will show liberty crushed everywhere between standing armies and perpetual taxes. The fortunes of a disunited America will be even more disastrous than Europe's. In Europe the sources of evil are confined within her own borders. No superior powers from another quarter of the globe intrigue among her rival nations, inflame their mutual animosities and turn them into instruments of foreign ambition, jealousy and revenge. In America, the miseries springing from her internal jealousies, contentions and wars would make up only part of her lot. A large additional share of evils would come from the relation in which Europe stands to this quarter of the earth, a relation no other quarter of the earth has to Europe.

This picture of the consequences of disunion cannot be painted too vividly or shown too often. Every man who loves peace, his country or liberty ought to keep it always before his eyes, so that he may feel in his heart a proper attachment to the Union of America and know the right value of the means of preserving it.

After the effective establishment of the Union, the best precaution against the danger of standing armies is to limit the term for which revenue may be appropriated to their support. The Constitution has wisely added this precaution. I will not repeat the observations that, I flatter myself, have put this subject in a just and satisfactory light. But it may be worth noticing an argument against this part of the Constitution that has been drawn from the policy and practice of Great Britain. It is said that keeping an army in that kingdom requires a vote of the legislature every year, while the American Constitution has stretched this critical period to two years. That is how the comparison is usually put before the public. But is the comparison put fairly? Does the British Constitution limit Parliament's discretion to one year? Does the American Constitution require Congress to make appropriations for two years? On the contrary, the authors of the fallacy cannot be unaware that the British Constitution sets no limit at all on the legislature's discretion, while the American Constitution binds the legislature to two years as the longest permitted term.

If the argument from the British example had been stated truly, it would have gone like this. The term for which supplies may be appropriated to the army, though the British Constitution leaves it unlimited, has nevertheless been limited in practice to a single year by Parliament's own discretion. Now consider Great Britain, where the House of Commons is elected for seven years, where so large a share of its members are chosen by so small a share of the people, where the electors are so corrupted by the representatives and the representatives so corrupted by the Crown. If the representative body there can have the power to make appropriations for the army for an indefinite term, and yet either does not wish to or does not dare to extend the term beyond one year, then ought not suspicion itself to blush when it pretends that the representatives of the United States cannot safely be trusted with discretion over such appropriations, though they are elected FREELY by the WHOLE BODY of the people every SECOND YEAR and the appropriations are expressly limited to the short period of TWO YEARS?

A bad cause seldom fails to give itself away. The way the opposition to the federal government has been conducted is a constant illustration of this truth. But of all the blunders committed, none is more striking than the attempt to bring over to that side the prudent jealousy the people feel toward standing armies. The attempt has fully awakened public attention to that important subject, and has led to inquiries that must end in a thorough and universal conviction of two things. One is that the Constitution has provided the most effective guards against danger from that quarter. The other is that only a Constitution fully adequate to the national defense and the preservation of the Union can save America from having as many standing armies as it is split into States or Confederacies, and from a steady growth of these establishments in each. Such growth would make them as burdensome to the property, and as ominous to the liberties, of the people as any establishment that might become necessary under a united and effective government would be tolerable to the one and safe to the other.

The plain necessity of the power to provide and maintain a navy has shielded that part of the Constitution from the spirit of censure that has spared few other parts. It must indeed be counted among the greatest blessings of America that, since her Union will be the only source of her naval strength, this strength will in turn be a chief source of her security against danger from abroad. In this respect our situation resembles in another way the island advantage of Great Britain. Happily, the batteries best able to repel foreign attempts on our safety are of a kind that a treacherous government can never turn against our liberties.

The inhabitants of the Atlantic frontier all have a deep interest in this provision for naval protection. They have been allowed so far to sleep quietly in their beds; their property has stayed safe from the plundering spirit of lawless adventurers; their seaport towns have not yet had to buy off the terror of burning by giving in to the demands of bold and sudden invaders. These pieces of good fortune are not to be credited to the existing government's ability to protect the people from whom it claims allegiance, but to causes that are passing and deceptive. Except perhaps for Virginia and Maryland, which are especially exposed on their eastern frontiers, no part of the Union ought to feel more anxiety on this subject than New York. Her seacoast is long. A very important district of the State is an island. A large navigable river runs into the State for more than fifty leagues. The great emporium of her commerce, the great reservoir of her wealth, lies every moment at the mercy of events, and may almost be regarded as a hostage for shameful compliance with the orders of a foreign enemy, or even with the greedy demands of pirates and barbarians. If war should result from the uncertain state of European affairs, and all the unruly passions that go with war were let loose on the ocean, it would be truly a miracle if we escaped insults and plundering, not only at sea but along every part of the land bordering on it. In America's present condition, the States most directly exposed to these calamities have nothing to hope for from the phantom of a general government that now exists. And if their own separate resources were equal to fortifying themselves against the danger, the thing to be protected would be nearly eaten up by the cost of protecting it.
The power of regulating and calling forth the militia has already been defended and explained sufficiently.

The power of levying and borrowing money is the sinew of the power to be used for the national defense, and is therefore rightly placed in the same class. This power too has already been examined with close attention, and I trust it has been clearly shown to be necessary, in both the extent and the form the Constitution gives it. I will offer only one further thought to those who argue that the power should have been limited to external taxation, by which they mean taxes on articles imported from other countries. There can be no doubt that this will always be a valuable source of revenue, that for a good while it must be a principal source, and that at this moment it is an essential one. But we may form very mistaken ideas on this subject if our calculations do not keep in mind two things. First, the amount of revenue drawn from foreign commerce must rise and fall with changes in both the amount and the kind of imports. Second, these changes do not match the growth of population, which must be the general measure of the public's needs. As long as agriculture remains the only field of labor, imports of manufactured goods must grow as consumers multiply. As soon as domestic manufactures begin, with hands that agriculture does not need, imported manufactures will fall as the population grows. At a later stage, imports may consist in large part of raw materials that will be worked up into articles for export, and these will need the encouragement of bounties rather than the burden of discouraging duties. A system of government meant to last ought to look ahead to these changes and be able to adapt to them.

Some who have not denied that the power of taxation is necessary have launched a very fierce attack on the Constitution over the language in which it is defined. It has been urged and echoed that the power "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States," amounts to an unlimited commission to exercise any power that may be claimed necessary for the common defense or general welfare. There could be no stronger proof of how hard up these writers are for objections than their stooping to such a misreading.

If the Constitution had contained no other listing or definition of the powers of Congress than the general expressions just quoted, the authors of the objection might have had some color for it, though it would still have been hard to find a reason for describing an authority to legislate in all possible cases in so awkward a way. A power to destroy the freedom of the press or trial by jury, or even to regulate the order of inheritance or the forms of conveyances, would be a very odd thing to express by the words "to raise money for the general welfare."

But what color can the objection have when a specification of the objects hinted at by these general terms follows right away, separated from them by no more than a semicolon? Different parts of the same document ought to be interpreted so as to give meaning to every part that can bear one. Shall one part of the same sentence then be shut out entirely from any share in the meaning, while the more doubtful and indefinite terms are kept in their full breadth and the clear and precise expressions are denied any meaning at all? Why would the list of particular powers have been inserted, if these and all other powers were meant to be included in the general power before it? Nothing is more natural or common than to use a general phrase first and then to explain and qualify it by listing particulars. But the idea of a list of particulars that neither explains nor qualifies the general meaning, and can have no effect except to confuse and mislead, is an absurdity. We are forced into a dilemma: we must charge it either to the authors of the objection or to the authors of the Constitution, and we must take the liberty of supposing it did not originate with the latter.

The objection is all the more extraordinary because the language the Convention used turns out to be copied from the articles of Confederation. The objects of the Union among the States, as described in article third, are "their common defense, security of their liberties, and mutual and general welfare." The terms of article eighth are closer still: "All charges of war and all other expenses that shall be incurred for the common defense or general welfare, and allowed by the United States in Congress, shall be defrayed out of a common treasury," etc. Similar language appears again in article ninth. Read either of these articles by the rules that would justify the reading given to the new Constitution, and they give the existing Congress a power to legislate in all cases whatsoever. But what would have been thought of that assembly if it had seized on these general expressions, ignored the specifications that fix and limit their meaning, and exercised an unlimited power of providing for the common defense and general welfare? I appeal to the objectors themselves: would they in that case have used the same reasoning to justify Congress that they now use against the Convention? How hard it is for error to escape its own condemnation!
